title: Photography direction for a two-sided marketplace
excerpt: Photograph a concrete match the scarce side would recognize. Skip pictures that only create a mood, and skip any frame whose idea is two equal buttons and no story.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a calm interior that still has to earn its place beside a real match.
caption: A cream sofa, an abstract painting, and teal vases between two windows. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should marketplace photography show?
faqs.answer: Show one match a peer would recognize: the people or the materials, the job underway, and a fact such as a seat count, a rate, or a shift time. Put that frame near the first sentence. A mood, a skyline, or a symbolic image of two sides does not give the scarce side a reason to join.

faqs.question: How should we brief a photographer for a marketplace site?
faqs.answer: List five frames before the shoot: the match in progress, the scarce side's real tool, the trust step you actually run, the place you serve if place matters, and a portrait only with permission. Include the words the site already uses, and plan a center-weighted crop for the phone. Reject any frame you cannot caption in one honest line.

faqs.question: When is an illustration better than a photograph?
faqs.answer: Use a diagram or a labeled sample when privacy, timing, or the product itself makes a photograph misleading. A specific table, fee, or route can be drawn and labeled as a sample. An abstract drawing of two figures and two arrows repeats the problem of equal buttons with no story.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Good two-sided marketplace website photography shows a concrete match. A picture that could sit under any headline is not neutral. It argues that you have nothing particular to show, and the side you need first believes you.

Choose frames that name the two parties and the thing that moved between them. Reject a composition whose only idea is two equal buttons and no story. The pictures are part of the argument.

## A photograph is a claim

Every image on the page claims "this is what it is like." A stock handshake claims the market is a meeting about a market. A laptop on a marble desk claims the product is the mood of the office. A split screen with two silhouettes and two buttons claims the sides are interchangeable. None of those claims help a host, a carrier, or a worker judge the risk.

Nielsen Norman Group's work on page visits is blunt about time. People often decide in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be visible within about 10 seconds if you want them to stay. On a phone, that window is one picture and one sentence. If the picture does not contain the match, the sentence has to do all the work while fighting the picture. Most sentences lose that fight.

Brief the photograph the way you brief a paragraph. Who is in the frame. What job is underway. What a peer would recognize. What must not appear because it tells the wrong story. A mood board of textures is not a brief. It is a way to postpone the claim.

The W3C WCAG principles start with perceivable. A match locked inside an image, with no text, is easy to miss and impossible for someone who cannot see it. The picture can carry the feeling of the room. The names, the time, and the outcome still need to be in the words beside it. Alt text should describe the picture, not the slogan you wished the picture proved.

## What a match looks like in a frame

A usable frame includes evidence. A table set for a counted number of guests, with a menu a cook would recognize. A rate and a lane visible before a driver accepts, even if you stage the screen with sample data that is labeled as a sample. A shift posted with a start time and a neighborhood. The evidence can be ordinary. Ordinary is convincing.

Show the scarce side doing the job, not watching a presentation about the job. Hands plating. A dispatcher pointing at a board that has real columns. A clinician reading a chart the way they actually read a chart. Faces are optional. The work is not. If someone is identifiable, you need their permission, and you should be willing to say who they are or leave them out.

Avoid the fake UI that floats in a void unless the interface itself is the match and the numbers on it are honest. A glowing card that says "You earned $10,000" with no context is a claim you may have to retract. If you show a screen, show the decision on it: accept, decline, cap the seats, release the payout.

One strong frame at the top of the homepage is worth more than a carousel of six. Carousels hide the claim behind a rotation the visitor will not wait for. Pick the match you are recruiting this month. Replace the picture when the market you are seeding changes. Do not rotate through audiences and call it personalization.

## What to reject

Reject pictures that reassure the team and confuse the applicant.

Two people on opposite sides of a glass wall, meant to symbolize "two sides." A globe. A shipping container if you are not in freight, and even then only if the container is the actual job. A diverse huddle around a laptop with no readable work on the screen. Hands exchanging a credit card. A city skyline that says you are ambitious and does not say what you list.

Reject images that contain a second call to action inside the art. A photo of a billboard, a phone mockup with "Sign up" and "Learn more" in equal buttons, or a poster that repeats the homepage hero, doubles the decision. The page already has a join path. The picture should not invent another one, and it should not split the one you have.

Reject anything you cannot caption in one honest line. If the caption would have to say "representation of synergy," the frame is wrong. If the caption can say "Host locks eight seats before the booking opens," the frame is a candidate.

Keep a kill list in the brief so a well-meaning collaborator does not add the rejected frame back at the end "to make it warmer." Warmth is welcome when it is the warmth of a real kitchen. It is noise when it is a filter.

## Direct the shoot

A small shoot beats a large library of almosts. Decide the five frames before the day.

One frame of the match in progress. One frame of the scarce side's tool or material, close enough to be specific. One frame of the trust mechanism you actually run, such as a checklist, a license, or a payout record with private details covered. One frame of the city or room you serve, if place matters. One portrait of the accountable person, only if they agreed and the about page names them.

Give the photographer the vocabulary list from the navigation and the services page. If the word is "dinner" and not "experience," the table should look like dinner. Props that belong to a different industry will be read as the industry. A stethoscope on a tutoring site is not a metaphor. It is a mistake.

Sample data on screens needs a pass before the shutter. Names, addresses, and earnings in a mock have a way of being real-looking enough to be a privacy problem, or fake-looking enough to be a credibility problem. Use obviously sample labels when the product is not live. Use real structure either way: columns a peer expects, not lorem ipsum in a sans serif.

Plan for the crop you will actually ship. A wide frame that only works on a desktop hero will be cut on a phone until the match is gone. Shoot with space, and also shoot a version where the evidence sits in the center. The phone crop is the primary crop for this buyer.

## Sequence, crop, and caption

Place the match picture first, next to the sentence that states the match. Do not put a mood frame above the fold and the evidence three sections down. People who leave in the first seconds will leave with the mood.

Caption the image with the fact, not with a joke and not with a keyword. "Tuesday seating, eight guests, menu confirmed by the host." The caption can credit the source if the picture is licensed. Alt text describes what a person would see: the table, the count, the menu, not "best two-sided marketplace."

Do not set type across the only evidence in the frame. A headline over a face is a common template. A headline over the rate the driver needed to see is a broken proof. If the layout needs type on the image, put it in the empty part of the frame, and keep the evidence intact.

Motion is optional and often worse. A slow zoom that delays the match, or a loop of abstract shapes behind the join button, spends the seconds you had. If you move something, move it to reveal the evidence, and respect reduced motion. A still that is clear beats a sequence that is almost clear.

## When not to use a photograph

Some matches are clearer as a diagram with real labels, or as a single annotated screen. A payment split, a cancellation window, a territory boundary. Forcing those into a lifestyle photograph produces a confused scene and a caption that does the real work. Use the diagram. Style it like the rest of the site. Do not pretend it is a photo of a feeling.

Illustration is the honest choice when you cannot show the people, the addresses, or the product yet. Label it as a diagram or a sample. An illustration of a specific table for eight, with a specific fee structure, still counts as a concrete match. An illustration of two abstract figures and two arrows does not. That second drawing is the equal-button problem in ink.

Buy less art. A site with three accurate pictures and a quiet background will feel more serious than a site with a unique photograph in every section, half of which argue with the copy. The sections can be mostly type. Type is not a failure of design. Type is how the boundary and the price stay legible.

The frame that survives on a desk often dies in the first phone screen, where the crop and the join path have to share a few hundred pixels. That is the next decision, [the mobile visit for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).

If you want the pictures commissioned as part of the page, not as a separate mood, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).
